description: I’m Hamdan Sayed, Team Owner for Earth in Motion (Dancing with the SARs). Passionate about space tech and Earth observation, I specialize in web prototyping, data visualization, and translating NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into interactive apps. We already have a live prototype tracking floods, wildfires, glaciers, and subsidence—join us to level up our data pipelines and pitch! Seeking teammates skilled in remote sensing/GIS, frontend/UI, or video storytelling.
summary:
We developed Earth in Motion, an interactive web platform powered by NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission capabilities. Built around five structured modules—The Mission, Earth Explorer, Scientific Chapters, Radar Workbench, and Zoom to Issue—the application translates dual-frequency 24 cm L-band and 12 cm S-band SweepSAR telemetry into accessible visual intelligence. Through interactive radar physics demonstrations and target-lock case studies covering Brahmaputra floods, the Rim Fire, Gulf of Mexico oil slicks, Pine Island Glacier velocity, and Central Valley land subsidence, users explore how radar penetrates clouds, smoke, and darkness to measure surface changes.

This solution directly addresses the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by bridging the gap between complex orbital radar datasets and public comprehension without requiring specialized Geographic Information System (GIS) software. It is essential because cloud cover and darkness frequently obscure optical satellites during emergencies, whereas democratizing all-weather SAR insights empowers students, educators, and planners to monitor environmental hazards and planetary surface dynamics effectively.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Earth in Motion is an interactive scientific web platform powered by NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission capabilities. Designed to bridge the gap between complex orbital radar telemetry and public understanding, the platform guides users through five structured modules: 01. The Mission, 02. Earth Explorer, 03. Scientific Chapters, 04. Radar Workbench, and 05. Zoom to Issue.

The application explains and visualizes NISAR's dual-frequency radar architecture:

  • 24 cm L-Band Antenna: Penetrates dense forest canopies and dry soil to expose woody structure and the ground beneath vegetation.
  • 12 cm S-Band Antenna: Scatters from the outermost surface layer to resolve rock, crops, and built structures with a finer, shallower signature.
  • SweepSAR Technology: Steers the radar beam across a 240 km swath width on a repeating 12-day global orbit without gaps between passes, capturing surface motion finer than a fingertip through clouds, smoke, and darkness.

In the Zoom to Issue module, users engage with interactive target-lock analyses grounded in NISAR Level-2 data products (NISAR_L2_GCOV, NISAR_L2_GOFF, and NISAR_L2_GUNW) across global hazard zones:

  • Flood Intelligence — Brahmaputra (26.20° N, 91.50° E): Highlights water inundation beneath cloud cover using specular HH reflection (NISAR_L2_GCOV, Ascending Track 84).
  • Wildfire & Forest Change — Rim Fire (37.85° N, 120.05° W): Tracks pre- and post-disaster vegetation structure via HV depolarization loss (NISAR_L2_GOFF, Descending Track 27).
  • Oil Slicks — Gulf of Mexico (27.40° N, 90.60° W): Analyzes ocean surface roughness damping (NISAR_L2_GCOV, Ascending Track 61, Coherence 0.31).
  • Glacial Motion — Pine Island Glacier (75.00° S, 100.00° W): Measures ice dynamics and rapid glacial flow via speckle and offset tracking (NISAR_L2_GOFF, Descending Track 119, Coherence 0.71).
  • Land Subsidence — Central Valley (36.50° N, 119.60° W): Monitors aquifer compaction and infrastructure risk through differential InSAR phase unwrapping (NISAR_L2_GUNW, Ascending Track 33, Coherence 0.83).

Key Benefits

  • Zero-Installation Browser Access: Eliminates the need for specialized Geographic Information System (GIS) software, command-line processing tools, or high-performance local workstations.
  • All-Weather, Day-and-Night Insight: Demonstrates how radar overcomes atmospheric barriers—such as monsoon cloud cover and wildfire smoke—that frequently obstruct traditional optical satellites.
  • Transparent Radar Physics: Connects observable environmental hazards directly to underlying physical mechanisms, including specular reflection, depolarization, interferometric coherence, and phase unwrapping.

Intended Impact

The primary objective of Earth in Motion is to democratize NASA and ISRO open Earth-observation science. By converting abstract orbital mechanics and interferometric radar principles into an intuitive, interactive browser experience, the platform empowers students and educators to explore real-world geophysics in the classroom while helping communities and urban planners understand how satellite radar monitors floods, wildfires, ice loss, and ground subsidence.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Application Development & Hosting: Base44 web development platform utilizing modern frontend web technologies (React, TypeScript/JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3) deployed live at [https://earth-in-motion-nasa.base44.app/](https://earth-in-motion-nasa.base44.app/).
  • Scientific & Mission Data References: NASA-ISRO NISAR mission specifications, orbital pass geometry parameters, and Level-2 data product structures (NISAR_L2_GCOV, NISAR_L2_GOFF, NISAR_L2_GUNW).
  • Documentation & Collaboration Software: GitHub for open-source repository management and Markdown documentation, presentation design software for the 7-slide pitch deck, and digital video editing tools for the 30-second demonstration.
  • Hardware: Standard team laptops and personal workstations used for interface prototyping, scientific verification, and media production.

Creativity and Innovation

Rather than presenting static academic text or raw radar backscatter matrices, Earth in Motion combines a live orbital telemetry aesthetic with guided scientific storytelling. The "Target Lock" spatial interface pairs animated radar physics diagrams with authentic satellite pass tracks, coordinates, and coherence values, allowing users to visually grasp how invisible millimeter-scale surface shifts are detected from orbit.

Factors Considered by the Team

  • Scientific Accuracy and Limitations: Our team prioritized technical fidelity by integrating real-world radar caveats directly into the user interface—for example, explicitly warning users that low-wind biogenic films can mimic oil slick signatures in marine radar imagery.
  • Progressive Learning Curve: We structured the navigation sequentially—moving from mission fundamentals and dual-band antenna physics to applied regional case studies—so users without prior remote-sensing experience can build comprehension step by step.
  • Accessibility and Bandwidth: Because raw SAR data granules are multi-gigabyte files, we engineered a lightweight, responsive web interface that delivers instant visual feedback on standard consumer devices and school internet connections.
